Wald test of a linear hypothesis on the graph layer

Source: R/wald.R
mc_wald_graph.Rd

Tests \(H_0:\mathbf L\boldsymbol\theta=\mathbf c\) on the parameters of the graph layer by the generalized Wald statistic, $$W=(\mathbf L\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}-\mathbf c)^\top \left[\mathbf L\,\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})\, \mathbf L^\top\right]^{-1}(\mathbf L\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}-\mathbf c),$$ referred to a chi-squared distribution with as many degrees of freedom as the rank of \(\mathbf L\). The covariance \(\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})\) is any of the three forms of mc_vcov_graph: model-based, sandwich, or sandwich corrected for the first stage.

Usage

mc_wald_graph(
  fit,
  L,
  rhs = 0,
  type = c("sandwich", "model", "two_stage"),
  cluster = NULL,
  small_sample = FALSE,
  method = c("auto", "shortcut", "full")
)

Arguments

fit

an object of class "mcglm_graph".

L

the contrast: a numeric matrix with one column per graph parameter, in the order of coef(fit, type = "graph") (or with those names as column names, in any order); a numeric vector, read as one row; or a character vector of parameter names, which selects them.

rhs

the right-hand side \(\mathbf c\), a single number or one value per row of L.

type

the covariance: "sandwich" (default), "model" or "two_stage", as in mc_vcov_graph.

cluster

optional vector with one identifier per observational row. With type = "sandwich" or "two_stage", the contributions are summed within clusters before the variability is formed, which is the form to use when the unit of dependence is not the row of the data matrix. It must have no missing value and at least two distinct values; the default NULL takes the rows as the units. It is refused with type = "model".

small_sample

logical, default FALSE; multiply the clustered variability by \(G/(G-1)\), with \(G\) the number of clusters. It has no effect without cluster and is refused with type = "model".

method

for type = "two_stage", the route of the correction, "auto" (default), "shortcut" or "full", as in mc_vcov_graph. It has no meaning for the other two types and is refused with them when it is not "auto".

Value

An object of class "htest": the Wald statistic \(W\) (named "X-squared"); parameter, the degrees of freedom df, equal to the rank of L; the p.value; the estimate \(\mathbf L\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\) and the null.value \(\mathbf c\), both named by the rows of L; the method and data.name labels; the numeric matrix contrast used, with one row per row of L and one column per graph parameter; and the covariance type.

Details

Let \(q=\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf L)\). Under \(H_0\), with the number of responses fixed and the number of units \(n\to\infty\), the asymptotic normality of \(\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}-\boldsymbol\theta_0)\) with covariance \(\mathbf J^{-1}\mathbf V\mathbf J^{-\top}\) gives \(\sqrt n(\mathbf L\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}-\mathbf c)\xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\boldsymbol\Xi)\), with \(\boldsymbol\Xi=\mathbf L\mathbf J^{-1}\mathbf V\mathbf J^{-\top} \mathbf L^\top\) positive definite when \(\mathbf J\) is nonsingular and \(\mathbf V\) is positive definite; \(W\) then converges to \(\chi^2_q\) once \(\boldsymbol\Xi\) is replaced by a consistent estimator. For a single edge, \(W=\hat\theta_e^2/ \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\theta_e)\) and \(q=1\). The sensitivity \(\mathbf J\) is the expected one in the GGM layer, where it coincides with the curvature, and the observed curvature of the working criterion in the DAG layer. With cluster, the contributions are summed within independent clusters before the variability is formed, and the asymptotic statement is in the number of clusters.

Scale

The statistic can be written with a per-unit curvature and variability, \(W=n(\mathbf L\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}-\mathbf c)^\top[\mathbf L \mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf V\mathbf H^{-\top}\mathbf L^\top]^{-1} (\mathbf L\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}-\mathbf c)\), with \(\mathbf H\) the observed curvature of the graph block, equal to the expected sensitivity \(\mathbf J\) in the GGM layer. The covariance returned by mc_vcov_graph is already on the scale of \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\), \(\mathbf H_n^{-1}(n\mathbf V) \mathbf H_n^{-1}=n^{-1}\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf V\mathbf H^{-1}\), so the two expressions are the same number.

A contrast that is not of full rank

Redundant rows add no restriction. The statistic is then formed on the range of \(\mathbf L\,\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}\,\mathbf L^\top\) and the degrees of freedom are the rank of \(\mathbf L\); a right-hand side that the redundant rows contradict is refused. The statistic is invariant to any invertible recombination of the rows, applied to \(\mathbf L\) and \(\mathbf c\) alike.

A contrast without variability

A hypothesis is refused when the covariance of the contrast is singular on its range, judged against the model-based variance of the same contrast. That happens with type = "two_stage" for a parameter the first stage fixes exactly, such as the innovation variance of a root node of a DAG with Gaussian intercept-only margins, whose corrected variance is zero. A contrast counts as having no variability when its variance is at most \(10^{-6}\) of its model-based variance, on the scale of the model-based standard deviations; the margin covers the numerical residue that the full form leaves where the exact variance is zero.

What the reference distribution requires

The chi-squared reference holds for a hypothesis fixed before looking at the data, under the regularity of the second-order estimating functions and, with type = "model", the working identity \(\mathbf V=\mathbf J\). Applied to parameters of a support chosen by a search over graphs, it is descriptive. Hypotheses on the first stage, the regression and dispersion parameters, are outside this function, which acts on the graph layer only; the htmcglm package tests those.

References

Godambe, V. P. (1960). An optimum property of regular maximum likelihood estimation. Annals of Mathematical Statistics 31(4), 1208–1211. doi:10.1214/aoms/1177705693

de Freitas, L. A. C. and Bonat, W. H. (2022). Hypothesis tests for multiple responses regression models in R: the htmcglm package. arXiv preprint arXiv:2208.01568. doi:10.48550/arXiv.2208.01568

See also

mc_test_independence and mc_test_adequacy, which are this test with a particular contrast, and mc_vcov_graph for the covariance.

Other inference on the graph layer: mc_test_adequacy(), mc_test_independence(), mc_two_stage_available(), mc_vcov_graph()

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(1); n <- 300
K <- diag(3) * 2; K[1, 2] <- K[2, 1] <- -0.7
Y <- matrix(rnorm(n * 3), n) %*% chol(solve(K))
d <- data.frame(y1 = Y[, 1], y2 = Y[, 2], y3 = Y[, 3], x = rnorm(n))
f <- mcglm_graph(list(y1 ~ x, y2 ~ x, y3 ~ x), data = d)
#> Automatic initial values selected.
mc_wald_graph(f, c("eta_13", "eta_23"))          # two edges at once
#> 
#> 	Wald test of 2 linear restrictions on the graph layer (sandwich
#> 	covariance)
#> 
#> data:  GGM layer with 6 parameters
#> X-squared = 1.0683, df = 2, p-value = 0.5862
#> sample estimates:
#> [1] -0.02798634 -0.04495199
#> 
mc_wald_graph(f, c(1, -1, 0, 0, 0, 0))           # eta_11 = eta_22
#> 
#> 	Wald test of 1 linear restriction on the graph layer (sandwich
#> 	covariance)
#> 
#> data:  GGM layer with 6 parameters
#> X-squared = 9.5848e-05, df = 1, p-value = 0.9922
#> sample estimates:
#> [1] -0.001224771
#> 
# }
